title: Atomics and Memory Ordering
summary: Count with std::atomic, publish data with release and acquire, update with compare_exchange, and pad away false sharing, checked against real assembly.
intro: A mutex makes any group of fields safe, but for one shared integer or flag it's heavy machinery. `std::atomic` makes single reads, writes, and read-modify-writes indivisible in hardware. This lesson counts with atomics, publishes data between threads, builds lock-free updates, and keeps threads from slowing each other through a shared cache line. Each claim about cost is checked against the assembly from the sandbox's g++ 10.2 (x86-64) and from Apple clang on a Mac (ARM64).

steps.title: Atomic counters
steps.body:
A risk counter or an order-id generator is one integer that every thread bumps. `std::atomic<int64_t>` from `<atomic>` makes each read-modify-write indivisible, so no update is lost and no lock is needed:

```cpp
std::atomic<int64_t> fills{0};
const int64_t before = fills.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
std::cout << before << ' ' << fills.load() << '\n';  // 0 1
```

`fetch_add` returns the old value, and `++fills` works too. The second argument is a **memory order**, the subject of the next part. Relaxed promises only that the count itself is exact, all a counter needs. Lore says relaxed is several times faster than the default, seq_cst. Not on x86-64: the `lock` prefix already orders all memory around it, so g++ 10.2 in the sandbox makes the same instruction for both:

```text
count_relaxed:
        lock add        QWORD PTR fills[rip], 1
        ret
count_seq_cst:
        lock add        QWORD PTR fills[rip], 1
        ret
```

On an Apple Silicon Mac, Apple clang makes `ldadd` for relaxed and `ldaddal`, which also orders memory, for seq_cst, so there the order can cost something:

```text
_count_relaxed:
        adrp    x8, _fills@PAGE
        add     x8, x8, _fills@PAGEOFF
        mov     w9, #1
        ldadd   x9, x8, [x8]
        ret
_count_seq_cst:
        adrp    x8, _fills@PAGE
        add     x8, x8, _fills@PAGEOFF
        mov     w9, #1
        ldaddal x9, x8, [x8]
        ret
```

An atomic covers one object, so a price and size that change together still need a mutex. You already use atomics, too: a `std::shared_ptr` copy adds 1 to the reference count, and its destructor subtracts 1. Pass one by value to a function that reads a single `double` through it, and g++ wraps that load in two locked instructions once the program has threads:

```text
.L22:
        lock add        DWORD PTR [rdx], 1
        movsd   xmm0, QWORD PTR [rax]
        test    rbx, rbx
        je      .L20
.L23:
        mov     eax, -1
        lock xadd       DWORD PTR [rdx], eax
        cmp     eax, 1
        jne     .L5
```

`lock xadd` with -1 also returns the old count, to see whether this was the last owner. On a hot path, pass a `shared_ptr` by `const&`, or `std::move` it to hand it over.

example.title: Mutex and atomic counters
example.prompt: Read k and n, let k threads count n messages each, once through a mutex and once with a relaxed fetch_add, and print both totals.
example.explanation: Four handlers count 250,000 messages each, so both totals are exactly 10^6 on every run. The atomic needs no lock, because each `fetch_add` is one `lock add` that no other core can split. Built with `// -O2` as the first line, four threads counting a million each took about 170 ms through the mutex here and about 40 ms with `fetch_add`, relaxed and seq_cst alike, rough times from the emulated sandbox. `counted.load()` runs after the joins, so even a relaxed count is complete by then.

practice.title: Unique order ids
practice.prompt:
Several gateway threads hand out order ids, and every id must be unique. Take each one with a single `fetch_add`.

1. In the loop, set `id` to `next_id.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed)`.
2. The rest is done: `main` reads `k n first_id`, collects every gateway's ids, sorts them, and prints how many there are, the first and the last, whether they're unique, and the next free id.

Input:

```text
4 50000 1000
```

Expected output:

```text
ids 200000
first 1000 last 200999
unique yes
next 201000
```

tests.output:
ids 200000
first 1000 last 200999
unique yes
next 201000

ids 21
first 1 last 21
unique yes
next 22

ids 200000
first 500000 last 699999
unique yes
next 700000

hints: `fetch_add` returns the value before the add, so the first id handed out is `first_id`.
Replace `const int64_t id = 0;` with `const int64_t id = next_id.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);`.
A separate `load()` and then `store()` would let two gateways read the same id. One `fetch_add` can't.

steps.title: Acquire, release, and seq_cst
steps.body:
A pricing thread writes a market snapshot, then flips a ready flag. A strategy thread that sees the flag must see the whole snapshot too, as the strategy process of *Processes Working Together: fork, Pipes, and Shared Memory* had to find each tick in its slot once it loaded the new `tail`:

```cpp harness
#include <bits/stdc++.h>

int main() {
    double snap = 0.0;
    std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
    {{code}}
    return 0;
}
```

```cpp
std::thread pricer([&] {
    snap = 4512.25;                                // plain writes first
    ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);  // then publish
});
while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {
}
std::cout << snap << '\n';  // 4512.25
pricer.join();
```

A **release** store keeps the writes before it from moving after it. An **acquire** load keeps the reads after it from moving before it. So once the acquire reads the released value, everything written before the release is visible, and this can never print 0. **Relaxed** orders nothing else, so a relaxed flag can arrive before the data. **seq_cst**, the default, also puts all seq_cst operations in one order that every thread agrees on. Two threads that each stored their own flag with release, then loaded the other's with acquire, both read `false` in more than 99% of 200,000 rounds here. With seq_cst, never.

g++ 10.2 in the sandbox (x86-64):

```text
publish_relaxed:
        mov     BYTE PTR ready[rip], 1
        ret
publish_release:
        mov     BYTE PTR ready[rip], 1
        ret
publish_seq_cst:
        mov     eax, 1
        xchg    al, BYTE PTR ready[rip]
        ret
```

Apple clang on an Apple Silicon Mac (ARM64):

```text
_publish_relaxed:
        mov     w8, #1
        adrp    x9, _ready@PAGE
        strb    w8, [x9, _ready@PAGEOFF]
        ret
_publish_release:
        adrp    x8, _ready@PAGE
        add     x8, x8, _ready@PAGEOFF
        mov     w9, #1
        stlrb   w9, [x8]
        ret
_publish_seq_cst:
        adrp    x8, _ready@PAGE
        add     x8, x8, _ready@PAGEOFF
        mov     w9, #1
        stlrb   w9, [x8]
        ret
```

x86 keeps stores in order and loads in order, so release costs nothing there, and the `xchg` stops a later load from passing the store. Loads are a plain `mov` in every order, while ARM64 uses `ldrb`, `ldaprb`, and `ldarb` for relaxed, acquire, and seq_cst. Relaxed compiling like release on x86 doesn't make it correct: the compiler may still move your writes past it, and ARM's hardware will.

example.title: Publishing a market snapshot
example.prompt: Read spot, volatility, and rate, publish them from a pricer thread with a release store, and let a strategy thread wait with an acquire load and price from them.
example.explanation: `pricer` copies the snapshot into `snap` with plain writes, then sets `ready` with a release store. `strategy` spins until its acquire load reads `true`, and from then on it's guaranteed to see all three fields, so it prices from 4512.25, 0.18, and 0.05: a 3-month forward of 4569.01 and a one-day move of 51.16. `main` reads `forward` and `daily_move` only after `join()`, which orders those reads too. Spinning keeps a core busy, which a hot path accepts in order to react within nanoseconds.

practice.title: Publishing risk limits
practice.prompt:
A risk thread publishes the day's limits, and the order gateway must not check a single order before they arrive.

1. In `risk`, copy `input` into `limits`, then store `true` to `armed` with `std::memory_order_release`.
2. In `gateway`, spin with `while (!armed.load(std::memory_order_acquire))` and an empty body before the loop over `orders`.
3. The rest is done: `main` reads the two limits, `n`, and the order sizes, joins both threads, and prints the counts and the final position.

Input:

```text
500 1200 6
300 600 200 400 100 300
```

Expected output:

```text
accepted 4
rejected 2
position 1000
```
hints: Without the wait, the gateway checks orders against limits of 0 and rejects every one.
The order matters: `limits = input;` comes before the release store, never after it.

steps.title: Compare-exchange loops
steps.body:
Some updates aren't additions. A risk system tracks the high-water mark of the day's P&L across threads, and a kill switch must fire exactly once, however many threads see the breach. `compare_exchange` does both without a lock: it stores a new value only if the atomic still holds the value you expected.

```cpp
void update_max(std::atomic<int64_t>& best, int64_t v) {
    int64_t cur = best.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    while (v > cur && !best.compare_exchange_weak(cur, v, std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
    }
}

std::atomic<int64_t> best{100};
update_max(best, 250);
std::cout << best.load() << '\n';  // 250
```

If `best` still equals `cur`, it becomes `v` and the call returns `true`. Otherwise another thread got there first: the call loads the current value into `cur` and returns `false`, and the loop tests `v > cur` again. g++ 10.2 in the sandbox makes a `lock cmpxchg` loop (x86-64):

```text
update_max:
        mov     rax, QWORD PTR [rdi]
.L3:
        cmp     rsi, rax
        jle     .L1
        lock cmpxchg    QWORD PTR [rdi], rsi
        jne     .L3
.L1:
        ret
```

Apple clang on the Mac makes a `cas` loop (ARM64):

```text
_update_max:
        ldr     x9, [x0]
        cmp     x1, x9
        b.le    LBB0_4
        mov     x8, x9
LBB0_2:
        cas     x8, x1, [x0]
        cmp     x8, x9
        b.eq    LBB0_4
        mov     x9, x8
        cmp     x1, x8
        b.gt    LBB0_2
LBB0_4:
        ret
```

The weak form may fail even when the values match, which happens on CPUs that build it from a load-exclusive and store-exclusive pair, like ARM64 chips without `cas`. So keep it in a loop. For a single try, use `compare_exchange_strong`:

```cpp
std::atomic<bool> killed{false};
bool expected = false;
if (killed.compare_exchange_strong(expected, true)) {
    std::cout << "this thread flipped the switch\n";
}
```

Exactly one thread gets `true`. Each later one finds `killed` already set, and `expected` comes back holding that `true`.

Retry such a claim in a loop and you have a **spinlock**, the smallest lock. `std::atomic_flag`, the one atomic type the standard guarantees lock-free, takes it with `while (f.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}` and frees it with `f.clear(std::memory_order_release)`. A waiter burns its core instead of sleeping, so a spinlock should guard only a few instructions.

A CAS compares only the value, not what happened in between, so a value that changed and changed back still passes. That's the ABA problem, which breaks a lock-free stack in *Beyond One Producer: MPMC Queues, ABA, and Seqlocks*, later in this section.

example.title: High-water mark and a kill switch
example.prompt: Read a loss limit and a day of P&L marks, let k threads track the high-water mark with a compare-exchange loop, and let the first thread to see a breach flip a kill switch.
example.output:
high water 7400
kill switch on, claims 1
example.explanation: Three threads scan four marks each, and every mark goes through `update_max`. The thread holding 7400 can lose a race, but each failed exchange reloads `cur` and tries again while 7400 is still bigger, so `high_water` always ends at 7400. Three marks fall below -5000, in two different threads' slices, so both threads try to flip `killed`. `compare_exchange_strong` lets exactly one of them win, so the claim count is always 1. Which thread wins changes from run to run, and the program never prints it.

practice.title: Best ask across feeds
practice.prompt:
Feed threads scan ask prices in ticks. Track the lowest ask with a compare-exchange loop, and raise one alert when an ask falls below `alert_below`.

1. Write `update_min`: load `best` relaxed into `cur`, then loop on `compare_exchange_weak` while `v < cur`.
2. In the thread, when `asks[j] < alert_below`, try `alerted.compare_exchange_strong(expected, true)` with `expected` starting at `false`, and add 1 to `alerts` only when it returns `true`.
3. The rest is done: `main` reads `k alert_below n` and the asks, then prints the best ask and the number of alerts.

Input:

```text
4 45100
12
45130 45128 45127 45131 45099 45126 45125 45129 45098 45124 45097 45130
```

Expected output:

```text
best ask 45097
alerts 1
```
hints: `update_min` is `update_max` from the example with `v < cur` in place of `v > cur`.
Declare `bool expected = false;` inside the loop, right before the exchange, because a failed exchange overwrites it.
Put both tests in one `if`: `asks[j] < alert_below && alerted.compare_exchange_strong(expected, true)`.

steps.title: False sharing and alignas

example.title: Packed and padded counters
example.prompt: Read k and n, let k threads each bump their own counter n times, first with counters packed side by side and then with each on its own cache line, and print the sizes and both totals.
example.output:
sizeof 8 and 64
alignof 8 and 64
packed 4000000
padded 4000000
example.explanation: Elements of a `std::vector` sit `sizeof` bytes apart, so the four packed counters fill 32 bytes in a row, one or two cache lines, and the padded ones start 64 bytes apart. The totals match: false sharing is never wrong, only slow. Here the packed run took about 80 ms, the padded one 10 to 30 ms, and the same counters padded to 128 bytes 3 to 14 ms, near one thread alone. These times are rough, since the sandbox runs x86-64 emulated on an Apple Silicon Mac, whose lines are 128 bytes: that's why 64 wasn't enough here.

practice.title: Padded P&L slots
practice.prompt:
Each book thread adds up the P&L of its slice of fills in its own slot. Pad the slots so that books never share a cache line.

1. Put `alignas(128)` on `PnlSlot`, so each slot takes 128 bytes.
2. Start `k` threads. Book `i` adds `fills[j]` into `slots[i].cents` for `j` from `n * i / k` up to but not including `n * (i + 1) / k`. Join them all.
3. The rest is done: `main` reads `k n` and the fills, then prints the slot size, each book's P&L, and the total.

Input:

```text
3 9
1250 -300 410 -2000 75 990 -15 600 -1200
```

Expected output:

```text
sizeof 128
book 0: 1360
book 1: -935
book 2: -615
total -190
```

tests.output:
sizeof 128
book 0: -5
book 1: -5
book 2: -5
book 3: -5
total -20

hints: Each slot is a plain `int64_t`: only book `i` writes `slots[i]`, so it needs no atomic, just its own line.
Capture `[&fills, &slots, i, k, n]`, and join with a loop over `books` before the printing.

recap:
- `std::atomic<int64_t>` makes `fetch_add`, `load`, and `store` indivisible. `fetch_add` returns the old value.
- On x86-64 a relaxed and a seq_cst `fetch_add` are the same `lock add`. On ARM64 they're `ldadd` and `ldaddal`.
- Copying a `std::shared_ptr` is an atomic increment and destroying the copy an atomic decrement, so pass it by `const&` or move it.
- Publish with a release store after the data, and read with an acquire load before using it.
- On x86-64, relaxed and release stores are a plain `mov`, a seq_cst store is an `xchg`, and every load is a `mov`. ARM64 uses ordered instructions, `stlrb`, `ldaprb`, and `ldarb`, for all but relaxed.
- seq_cst is the safe default. Use relaxed for a pure counter and release and acquire for a ready flag.
- `compare_exchange_weak` in a loop builds max, min, and other lock-free updates. `compare_exchange_strong` makes a once-only claim, and `std::atomic_flag` makes a spinlock.
- Data that different threads write often needs its own cache line: `alignas(64)` fits x86-64 servers, and `alignas(128)` is the safe pad when one binary must also suit Apple Silicon.

Next, **A Lock-Free SPSC Ring Buffer** builds on the release and acquire pair: the queue that carries ticks from one thread to the next with no lock and no allocation.
